OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) — Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, safely back in the United States after being attacked by pirates last week off the coast of Somalia, recounted their ordeal Thursday.

Navy personnel recovered the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday.

“They started firing before they climbed aboard, with AK-47s,” crew member Zahid Reza said. “I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times,” he said, pointing to his head. “Pointing guns all over. Here, there, in the back.”

Pirates tried three times to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before succeeding on their fourth attempt, fellow crew member William Rios said. He added that the groups of pirates appeared to be different, though he believed they were working together.

Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to help lock down the ship. Then, he said, gunshots rang out, and an alarm sounded to wake all crew members and direct them to get on deck.

“We went to our training,” he said, declining to provide details. “If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know.”

*Watch the crew praise their captain »*

The pirates intended to demand a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said he and the ship’s chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage.

Reza said he persuaded the pirate — whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19 — to trust him, noting that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali.

“His name is Abdul,” Reza said. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.’”

He told Abdul he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, Reza said, and he did not know the ship’s chief engineer was inside.

He said the chief engineer jumped the pirate first; then Reza stabbed him with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he intended to kill the youth, but the chief engineer told him, “No, we need him alive.”

*Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate »*

“He was fighting me and [the] chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he went to the lifeboat, where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held, to exchange Abdul for Phillips, but the attempt was unsuccessful.

Phillips — who offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew — was rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. The SEALs, positioned on the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested.

“I feel great they got killed,” Reza said. “I am happy.” He said he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips arrived Thursday in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge. The crew arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

*Watch crew arrive in U.S. »*

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding; he’s extraordinary; he’s [a] very brave man.”

Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios called for greater security in the Gulf of Aden.

“Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth,” he said. “... All the countries got to get involved with this.”

Reza echoed that call.

“I think government should get involved,” he said. “They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger.”

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) — After returning safely to the United States following a pirate attack off the coast of Somalia the previous week, crew members from the Maersk Alabama described their experience on Thursday.

U.S. Navy personnel retrieved the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued on Sunday.

Crewman Zahid Reza said the attackers opened fire with AK-47s even before climbing aboard. “I was afraid I was going to die,” he said. “I came very close.” Pointing toward his head, he added that the pirates attempted to shoot him several times and aimed their weapons in multiple directions — “here, there, in the back.”

Another crew member, William Rios, said pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to get onto the U.S.-flagged cargo vessel before succeeding on the fourth try. He said the pirates appeared to be from different groups, though he believed they were cooperating.

Rios said he had been working on deck when he was ordered back so the ship could be secured. Soon afterward, he said, shots were fired and an alarm sounded, warning the crew to wake up and report to the deck. He said the crew followed its training but would not explain the procedures, saying that if he revealed what they did, pirates would learn from it.

Reza said the hijackers planned to demand $3 million in ransom. He also said that he and the ship’s chief engineer captured one of the pirates.

According to Reza, he convinced the pirate — whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19 years old — to believe him by noting that he was from Bangladesh and Muslim, while the pirate was Somali and also Muslim. Reza said the pirate’s name was Abdul. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim,’” he said.

Reza said he told Abdul he would take him to the engine room to locate other crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, and Reza said he did not realize the chief engineer was inside. The chief engineer attacked the pirate first, Reza said, and then Reza stabbed him with a knife. The two men then bound the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he wanted to kill the young pirate, but the chief engineer stopped him, saying they needed him alive.

“He was struggling with me and the chief engineer, trying to break free,” Reza said. “There was a lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he later went to the lifeboat where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held and tried to trade Abdul for Phillips, but the exchange did not work.

Phillips, who had offered himself as a hostage so his crew could be released, was freed Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. The SEALs, positioned on the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, killed three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was taken into custody.

Reza said he was glad the three pirates were killed and expressed pride in the Navy.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. His crew arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding,” “extraordinary” and “a very brave man.” Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios urged stronger security in the Gulf of Aden, calling for more military patrols to protect ships moving goods through the area. He said all nations needed to participate.

Reza made a similar appeal, saying governments should become involved and pay more attention to crew safety. He warned that piracy was continuing to grow.

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

## After the Maersk Alabama Hijacking: Crew Recounts Ordeal as Capt. Phillips’ Rescue Ends Standoff

**MOMBASA, Kenya / Norfolk, Va. —** In the days after U.S. Navy SEAL snipers ended the dramatic hostage crisis involving the **Maersk Alabama**, crew members described a harrowing confrontation with Somali pirates, a tense attempt to retake control of their ship, and the relief that followed the rescue of **Capt. Richard Phillips**, who had been held for days in a covered lifeboat in the Indian Ocean.

The April 2009 hijacking of the U.S.-flagged cargo ship became one of the most closely watched piracy cases of the modern era. It exposed the dangers faced by merchant mariners off the Horn of Africa and prompted renewed debate over armed security, naval patrols, and the vulnerability of commercial shipping.

### The Attack and the Crew’s Response

The **Maersk Alabama**, carrying humanitarian aid and commercial cargo, was sailing off the coast of Somalia when a small pirate skiff approached. Despite evasive maneuvers and emergency procedures, four armed pirates boarded the vessel.

Crew members later described scrambling into secure areas of the ship, cutting power, and using the vessel’s layout to frustrate the attackers. The ship’s engineers and deck crew played a major role in preventing the pirates from fully controlling the vessel.

Several crew accounts emphasized that the pirates appeared confused once aboard and struggled to operate the large container ship. Members of the crew said they had trained for pirate attacks and used those drills to hide, disable systems, and communicate internally.

### Crew Interviews: Fear, Improvisation, and Relief

Crew members interviewed after the incident described a mix of fear and discipline. Some said they believed the pirates would kill them if they were discovered; others said the crew’s knowledge of the ship gave them an advantage.

The engineering crew was widely credited with helping neutralize the situation aboard the Maersk Alabama. By retreating into the engine room and other secure spaces, crew members deprived the pirates of easy access to the ship’s operations. At one point, crew members managed to capture one of the pirates who had gone below deck, creating leverage in negotiations.

After the crisis ended, many crew members expressed gratitude toward the U.S. Navy while also acknowledging the lasting psychological toll. Some later criticized aspects of company security policy, arguing that ships traveling near Somalia needed stronger protection.

### Zahid Reza’s Account

In accounts attributed to crewman **Zahid Reza**, the atmosphere aboard the Maersk Alabama was described as chaotic and frightening as the pirates moved through the vessel looking for crew members and control points. Reza’s account emphasized the crew’s reliance on training, teamwork, and the ship’s internal layout to stay ahead of the attackers.

According to such accounts, crew members were acutely aware that the pirates were armed and unpredictable. Reza described the crew remaining hidden and communicating carefully while the pirates searched the ship. Like other crew recollections, his version underscored that the ship was not simply “taken” without resistance; rather, the crew actively worked to deny the pirates full command of the vessel.

His account also reflected a broader theme repeated by crew members after the hijacking: the sailors felt they survived because they stayed organized, trusted one another, and refused to panic.

### Capt. Phillips Taken Hostage

The standoff shifted after Capt. Phillips agreed to leave the Maersk Alabama in a lifeboat with the pirates. Phillips later said he was trying to protect his crew and move the pirates away from the ship. The pirates took him hostage in the small enclosed lifeboat and attempted to make for the Somali coast.

The Maersk Alabama itself was freed, but Phillips remained captive for several days. The lifeboat was soon shadowed by U.S. naval forces, including the destroyer **USS Bainbridge**. Negotiators attempted to resolve the crisis while Navy commanders assessed the risk that the pirates might kill Phillips or reach Somalia, where a rescue would become far more difficult.

### The Captured Pirate: Abduwali Muse

One pirate, later identified as **Abduwali Abdukhadir Muse**, survived and was taken into U.S. custody. Muse became the only surviving pirate from the lifeboat standoff after the rescue operation.

He was brought to the United States for prosecution, an unusual and highly visible step at the time. Muse initially drew public attention because of questions about his age, with reports suggesting he may have been a teenager. U.S. authorities ultimately prosecuted him as an adult.

Muse later pleaded guilty to charges connected to piracy and hostage-taking. He was sentenced to more than 30 years in federal prison. His case became a landmark example of U.S. criminal prosecution for modern piracy and demonstrated that suspects captured in international waters could face trial in American courts.

### Navy SEAL Rescue of Capt. Phillips

The crisis reached its climax on **April 12, 2009**, when U.S. Navy SEAL marksmen aboard the USS Bainbridge opened fire on the pirates holding Phillips.

Navy officials said commanders acted after determining that Phillips’ life was in imminent danger. Three pirates were visible in the lifeboat, and SEAL snipers fired nearly simultaneous shots, killing all three. Phillips was rescued unharmed and brought aboard the Bainbridge.

The operation was widely praised for its precision. It also highlighted the role of naval special operations forces in counter-piracy missions and became one of the most prominent U.S. military rescue operations of the decade.

### Aftermath for Capt. Phillips and the Crew

Capt. Phillips returned home to national attention and was celebrated as a hero by many Americans. He later wrote a memoir, and the story was adapted into the 2013 film **“Captain Phillips,”** starring Tom Hanks.

However, some crew members later disputed portions of Phillips’ public account and argued that the captain and company had underestimated the pirate threat. Lawsuits and public statements from some crew members alleged that the vessel sailed too close to the Somali coast despite warnings. The company maintained that it followed appropriate procedures and emphasized the extraordinary danger posed by the pirates.

For the crew, the aftermath was complicated. While the rescue ended successfully, many sailors said the incident left emotional scars. The hijacking also intensified scrutiny of how commercial vessels prepared for piracy and whether crews should be protected by armed guards.

### Broader Impact on Maritime Security

The Maersk Alabama hijacking became a turning point in global awareness of Somali piracy. In the years that followed, shipping companies increasingly adopted security measures such as:

- armed security teams aboard vessels;
- reinforced safe rooms, known as citadels;
- evasive routing and speed adjustments;
- coordinated naval patrols;
- improved crew training and emergency communication systems.

International naval operations off Somalia expanded, and the shipping industry changed its approach to high-risk transit corridors. While piracy off Somalia later declined sharply, the Maersk Alabama incident remains one of the defining episodes of the era.

### A Crisis Remembered

The aftermath of the Maersk Alabama hijacking left several competing narratives: Phillips’ widely publicized story of sacrifice and survival, crew members’ accounts of collective resistance and frustration, Zahid Reza’s recollection of fear and teamwork below deck, and the legal saga of Abduwali Muse, the lone surviving pirate.

What remains undisputed is that the crisis ended with a rare and dramatic rescue at sea — one that saved Capt. Phillips, returned the crew home, and reshaped how the world viewed piracy in the 21st century.

**BREAKING NEWS: U.S.-Flagged Maersk Alabama Seized by Somali Pirates; Crew Fights Back, Captain Taken Hostage**

**NAIROBI, Kenya / WASHINGTON —** Somali pirates attacked the U.S.-flagged container ship **Maersk Alabama** off the Horn of Africa, sparking a dramatic confrontation at sea in which the crew fought back, regained control of their vessel, and saw their captain taken hostage in a lifeboat, officials and maritime sources said.

The attack on the **17,000-ton Maersk Alabama**, one of the most high-profile pirate assaults on an American merchant vessel in modern times, unfolded in waters plagued by piracy near Somalia, where armed gangs have repeatedly targeted commercial shipping routes linking Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

The ship, operated by Maersk Line Ltd., was carrying food aid and other cargo bound for East Africa when pirates approached in a small skiff and managed to board. The vessel’s crew, led by **Captain Richard Phillips**, initiated anti-piracy procedures, including evasive maneuvers and efforts to secure themselves inside the ship.

According to accounts from officials and crew members, the sailors did not passively submit. They cut power, retreated to secure areas, and used their knowledge of the ship to frustrate the attackers. At one point, crew members reportedly overpowered one of the pirates, raising the possibility of a trade for Phillips and forcing the attackers into a chaotic retreat.

Despite the crew’s resistance, Phillips was taken from the vessel by the pirates and held aboard one of the ship’s enclosed lifeboats. The captain’s capture set off a tense hostage crisis at sea, with U.S. military forces moving into the area as negotiators sought to secure his release.

The standoff drew urgent attention from Washington, where the incident was seen as a test of the United States’ ability to respond to the growing threat of piracy off Somalia.

The Maersk Alabama attack marked a rare seizure of a U.S.-flagged vessel and intensified calls from shipping companies, maritime unions and security experts for stronger protection of commercial ships transiting dangerous waters near Somalia, including the Gulf of Aden and the wider western Indian Ocean.

“This incident underscores the vulnerability of merchant crews operating in high-risk waters,” one maritime security analyst said. “Ships are moving through an area where pirates can launch attacks from small boats, often far from shore, and the response time can be critical.”

For years, Somali pirate groups have exploited instability on land and the vastness of surrounding sea lanes, using skiffs launched from larger “mother ships” to attack tankers, cargo ships and aid vessels. Crews have faced hijackings, ransom demands and months of captivity. The Gulf of Aden, a key corridor leading to the Suez Canal, has been one of the world’s most dangerous maritime chokepoints.
